claim: HIV establishes a persistent infection in heterogeneous cell reservoirs.
source: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) establishes a persistent infection in heterogeneous cell reservoirs, which can be maintained by different mechanisms including cellular proliferation, and represent the main obstacle to curing the infection.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about HIV persistence.

claim: HIV reservoirs can be maintained by cellular proliferation.
source: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) establishes a persistent infection in heterogeneous cell reservoirs, which can be maintained by different mechanisms including cellular proliferation, and represent the main obstacle to curing the infection.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is cited in the introduction.

claim: HIV reservoirs represent the main obstacle to curing the infection.
source: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) establishes a persistent infection in heterogeneous cell reservoirs, which can be maintained by different mechanisms including cellular proliferation, and represent the main obstacle to curing the infection.
evidence: This is a well-established concept in HIV research supported by scientific consensus.

claim: CD32 expression has been identified as a marker of active cell reservoirs in people on antiretroviral therapy.
source: The expression of the Fcγ receptor CD32 has been identified as a marker of the active cell reservoirs in people on antiretroviral therapy (ART), but if its expression has any role in conferring advantage for viral persistence is unknown.
evidence: This statement references prior research findings about CD32 as a reservoir marker.

claim: HIV-infected cells expressing CD32 have reduced susceptibility to natural killer antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity.
source: Here, we report that HIV-infected cells expressing CD32 have reduced susceptibility to natural killer (NK) antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity (ADCC) by a mechanism compatible with the suboptimal binding of HIV-specific antibodies.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The reduced susceptibility of CD32-expressing infected cells to ADCC is mediated by suboptimal binding of HIV-specific antibodies.
source: Here, we report that HIV-infected cells expressing CD32 have reduced susceptibility to natural killer (NK) antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity (ADCC) by a mechanism compatible with the suboptimal binding of HIV-specific antibodies.
evidence: This mechanism is proposed based on experimental data showing reduced antibody binding to CD32+ cells.

claim: Infected CD32 cells have increased proliferative capacity in the presence of immune complexes.
source: Infected CD32 cells have increased proliferative capacity in the presence of immune complexes, and are more resistant to strategies directed to potentiate NK function.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data showing Ki67 expression in CD32+ cells after immune complex engagement.

claim: Infected CD32 cells are more resistant to strategies directed to potentiate NK function.
source: Infected CD32 cells have increased proliferative capacity in the presence of immune complexes, and are more resistant to strategies directed to potentiate NK function.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that IL-15 and IFN-α treatment did not enhance killing of CD32+ cells.

claim: Reactivation of the latent reservoir from antiretroviral-treated people living with HIV increases the pool of infected CD32 cells.
source: Remarkably, reactivation of the latent reservoir from antiretroviral-treated people living with HIV increases the pool of infected CD32 cells, which are largely resistant to the ADCC immune mechanism.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data from latency reversal experiments showing increased CD32 expression on reactivated cells.

claim: Reactivated infected CD32 cells are largely resistant to the ADCC immune mechanism.
source: Remarkably, reactivation of the latent reservoir from antiretroviral-treated people living with HIV increases the pool of infected CD32 cells, which are largely resistant to the ADCC immune mechanism.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data showing that CD32+ cells remain or increase after ADCC assays.

claim: ART does not fully eliminate HIV from the human body.
source: Despite huge advances on the optimization of ART, which leads to suppression of viral replication, ART does not fully eliminate the virus from the human body nor can completely solve the persistent inflammation caused by HIV (Klatt et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Klatt et al., 2013 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: ART cannot completely solve the persistent inflammation caused by HIV.
source: Despite huge advances on the optimization of ART, which leads to suppression of viral replication, ART does not fully eliminate the virus from the human body nor can completely solve the persistent inflammation caused by HIV (Klatt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Klatt et al., 2013.

claim: ART discontinuation leads to viral rebound from diverse anatomical sites and cell subsets containing replication-competent viruses.
source: Importantly, ART discontinuation leads to viral rebound from diverse anatomical sites and cell subsets containing replication-competent viruses (Grau-Expósito et al., 2017; Jost and Altfeld, 2012; Madhavi et al., 2015) representing the main obstacle in achieving cure (Joos et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Central memory cells are one of the main populations contributing to the total reservoir size.
source: i.e., central memory cells are one of the main populations contributing to the total reservoir size (Chomont et al., 2009), effector memory cells support HIV transcription (Grau-Expósito et al., 2017) and contain higher proportions of intact viral regions (Duette et al., 2022; Musick et al., 2019; Hiener et al., 2017), and memory stem cells and resident memory T cells are potentially long-lived niches for HIV (Buzon et al., 2014; Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chomont et al., 2009.

claim: Effector memory cells support HIV transcription.
source: i.e., central memory cells are one of the main populations contributing to the total reservoir size (Chomont et al., 2009), effector memory cells support HIV transcription (Grau-Expósito et al., 2017) and contain higher proportions of intact viral regions (Duette et al., 2022; Musick et al., 2019; Hiener et al., 2017), and memory stem cells and resident memory T cells are potentially long-lived niches for HIV (Buzon et al., 2014; Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grau-Expósito et al., 2017.

claim: Effector memory cells contain higher proportions of intact viral regions.
source: i.e., central memory cells are one of the main populations contributing to the total reservoir size (Chomont et al., 2009), effector memory cells support HIV transcription (Grau-Expósito et al., 2017) and contain higher proportions of intact viral regions (Duette et al., 2022; Musick et al., 2019; Hiener et al., 2017), and memory stem cells and resident memory T cells are potentially long-lived niches for HIV (Buzon et al., 2014; Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Duette et al., 2022; Musick et al., 2019; Hiener et al., 2017.

claim: Memory stem cells and resident memory T cells are potentially long-lived niches for HIV.
source: i.e., central memory cells are one of the main populations contributing to the total reservoir size (Chomont et al., 2009), effector memory cells support HIV transcription (Grau-Expósito et al., 2017) and contain higher proportions of intact viral regions (Duette et al., 2022; Musick et al., 2019; Hiener et al., 2017), and memory stem cells and resident memory T cells are potentially long-lived niches for HIV (Buzon et al., 2014; Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Buzon et al., 2014; Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019.

claim: CD32 is a low-affinity receptor for the constant fraction of immunoglobulin G (FcγR-IIa).
source: In this regard, the molecule CD32, a low-affinity receptor for the constant fraction of immunoglobulin G (FcγR-IIa), was proposed as a marker of HIV reservoir cells (Descours et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a well-established biochemical property of CD32 supported by scientific knowledge.

claim: CD32 was proposed as a marker of HIV reservoir cells.
source: In this regard, the molecule CD32, a low-affinity receptor for the constant fraction of immunoglobulin G (FcγR-IIa), was proposed as a marker of HIV reservoir cells (Descours et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Descours et al., 2017.

claim: The original findings about CD32 as a reservoir marker were questioned due to identification of experimental artifacts.
source: While those results were questioned later by the identification of experimental artifacts (Bertagnolli et al., 2018; Pérez et al., 2018), several new studies partially corroborated the original findings; higher levels of viral DNA within the TCD32 population were reported after applying a very stringent cell isolation protocol (Darcis et al., 2020) and CD32 was identified as a marker of transcriptionally active persistent HIV-infected cells, both in blood and in the main reservoir tissues, namely the lymph nodes and the gastrointestinal tract (Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019; Abdel-Mohsen et al., 2018; Badia et al., 2018; Vásquez et al., 2019; Noto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bertagnolli et al., 2018; Pérez et al., 2018.

claim: Higher levels of viral DNA within the TCD32 population were reported after applying a very stringent cell isolation protocol.
source: While those results were questioned later by the identification of experimental artifacts (Bertagnolli et al., 2018; Pérez et al., 2018), several new studies partially corroborated the original findings; higher levels of viral DNA within the TCD32 population were reported after applying a very stringent cell isolation protocol (Darcis et al., 2020) and CD32 was identified as a marker of transcriptionally active persistent HIV-infected cells, both in blood and in the main reservoir tissues, namely the lymph nodes and the gastrointestinal tract (Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019; Abdel-Mohsen et al., 2018; Badia et al., 2018; Vásquez et al., 2019; Noto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Darcis et al., 2020.

claim: CD32 was identified as a marker of transcriptionally active persistent HIV-infected cells in blood and main reservoir tissues.
source: While those results were questioned later by the identification of experimental artifacts (Bertagnolli et al., 2018; Pérez et al., 2018), several new studies partially corroborated the original findings; higher levels of viral DNA within the TCD32 population were reported after applying a very stringent cell isolation protocol (Darcis et al., 2020) and CD32 was identified as a marker of transcriptionally active persistent HIV-infected cells, both in blood and in the main reservoir tissues, namely the lymph nodes and the gastrointestinal tract (Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019; Abdel-Mohsen et al., 2018; Badia et al., 2018; Vásquez et al., 2019; Noto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Infected CD4+ T cells expressing CD32 contain replication-competent HIV and are found in long-term ART-treated people living with HIV.
source: Importantly, whether or not CD32 is a marker of latent or transcriptionally active infection, infected CD4+ T cells expressing CD32 contain replication-competent HIV and are found in long-term ART-treated people living with HIV (PLWH) (Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019; Descours et al., 2017; Darcis et al., 2020; Abdel-Mohsen et al., 2018; Badia et al., 2018; Vásquez et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: CD20 has been shown to identify transcriptionally active HIV cells in samples from ART-suppressed PLWH.
source: The cell markers CD20 (Serra-Peinado et al., 2019) and CD30 (Hogan et al., 2018) have been shown to also identify transcriptionally active HIV cells in samples from ART-suppressed PLWH.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Serra-Peinado et al., 2019.

claim: CD30 has been shown to identify transcriptionally active HIV cells in samples from ART-suppressed PLWH.
source: The cell markers CD20 (Serra-Peinado et al., 2019) and CD30 (Hogan et al., 2018) have been shown to also identify transcriptionally active HIV cells in samples from ART-suppressed PLWH.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hogan et al., 2018.

claim: NK cells can eliminate cancer cells or virally-infected cells without prior antigen sensitization.
source: NK cells are lymphocytes that can eliminate cancer cells or virally-infected cells without prior antigen sensitization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NK cell biology.

claim: NK cells kill target cells by natural cytotoxicity, recognizing stress ligands expressed on the surface of infected cells.
source: NK cells kill target cells by several mechanisms, such as natural cytotoxicity (NC), recognizing stress ligands expressed on the surface of infected cells, or by ADCC, driven by antibodies that bind to target cells (Vivier et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vivier et al., 2008 and represents established knowledge.

claim: NK cells kill target cells by ADCC, driven by antibodies that bind to target cells.
source: NK cells kill target cells by several mechanisms, such as natural cytotoxicity (NC), recognizing stress ligands expressed on the surface of infected cells, or by ADCC, driven by antibodies that bind to target cells (Vivier et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vivier et al., 2008 and represents established knowledge.

claim: The decision of NK cells to kill or not to kill a target cell depends on the balance between activating and inhibitory signals received from the interaction with the target cell.
source: The decision of NK cells to kill or not to kill a target cell depends on the balance between activating and inhibitory signals received from the interaction with the target cell (Lanier, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lanier, 2008.

claim: Expression of the inhibitory receptor NKG2A is known to impact NK effector responses through its interaction with HLA-E molecules.
source: Further, expression of the inhibitory receptor NKG2A is known to impact NK effector responses through its interaction with HLA-E molecules (Bottino et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bottino et al., 2005.

claim: Therapeutic interventions blocking the NKG2A-HLA-E interaction represent promising tools to potentiate NK cell immune responses during different pathologies.
source: In this sense, therapeutic interventions blocking this interaction represent promising tools to potentiate NK cell immune responses during different pathologies (André et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to André et al., 2018; Pereira et al., 2019.

claim: HIV infection causes NK cell dysfunction, which is not completely restored by ART.
source: Importantly, HIV infection causes NK cell dysfunction, which is not completely restored by ART (Nabatanzi et al., 2019; Lichtfuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nabatanzi et al., 2019; Lichtfuss et al., 2012.

claim: NK cells play an important role in containing viral replication during early infection and shaping adaptive immune responses during chronic infection.
source: NK cells play an important role in containing viral replication during early infection and shaping adaptive immune responses during chronic infection (Flórez-Álvarez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Flórez-Álvarez et al., 2018.

claim: Proportions of NK cells inversely correlated with HIV-1 DNA reservoir levels in a clinical study designed to disrupt viral latency.
source: Moreover, proportions of NK cells inversely correlated with HIV-1 DNA reservoir levels in a clinical study designed to disrupt viral latency (Olesen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olesen et al., 2015.

claim: During chronic infection, HIV uses several strategies to evade NK cell immune responses, including the modulation of HLA class I molecules expression at the surface of infected cells.
source: Importantly, during chronic infection, several strategies used by HIV to evade NK cell immune responses have been described, including the modulation of HLA class I molecules expression at the surface of infected cells (Jost and Altfeld, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jost and Altfeld, 2012.

claim: Each CD4+ T cell subset had a different susceptibility to autologous NK cells, with TEM being most susceptible and TCD32dim being most resistant to ADCC.
source: Results showed that each CD4+ T cell subset had a different susceptibility to autologous NK cells, being TEM >TCM > TCD20dim>TNA>TSCM>TCD32dim more prone to be killed (ANOVA Friedman test p=0.0001) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A with statistical analysis.

claim: TCD32dim cells showed the highest resistance to ADCC among CD4+ T cell subsets.
source: Overall, most CD4+T cell subsets were susceptible to ADCC, however TCD32dim cells, and to a lesser extent TSCM, showed the highest resistance to ADCC.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from ADCC assays.

claim: A median of 1.21% of CD4+ T cells expressed the CD32 receptor.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Darcis et al., 2020; Abdel-Mohsen et al., 2018; Holgado et al., 2018; García et al., 2018), we found that a median of 1.21% of CD4+ T cells expressed the CD32 receptor, and no statistically significant differences were detected between ART-suppressed, EC participants and HD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to prior studies.

claim: There was no correlation between the HIV-DNA or HIV-RNA levels and the frequency of CD32 expression on CD4+ T cells.
source: In addition, and in concordance with the study of García et al., but differing from the report of Darcis et al. (Darcis et al., 2020; García et al., 2018), there was no correlation between the HIV-DNA or HIV-RNA levels and the frequency of CD32 expression on CD4+ T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E and citations.

claim: NK cells from healthy donors were highly efficient at killing the total CD4+ T cell population.
source: We observed that overall, NK cells from healthy donors were highly efficient at killing the total CD4+ T cell population (Figure 1B) and the different CD4+ T subsets (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Total CD4+ T cells as well as all subsets from ART-treated PLWH were less susceptible to ADCC-mediated killing than HD.
source: Total CD4+ T cells (Figure 1B) as well as all subsets from ART-treated PLWH were less susceptible to ADCC-mediated killing than HD (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: There was a statistically significant inverse correlation between the percentage of ADCC activity against CD4+ T cells and the total HIV-DNA reservoir size.
source: We observed a statistically significant inverse correlation between the percentage of ADCC activity against CD4+ T cells and the total HIV-DNA reservoir size (Figure 1D) and, in particular, for the ADCC against TCD32dim cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: After ex vivo infection of CD4+ T cells, higher expression of the CD32 molecule was observed in comparison to uninfected cells.
source: After the ex vivo infection of CD4+ T cells, we observed higher expression of the CD32 molecule in comparison to uninfected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: No significant differences between the killing of TCD32dim and TCD32− by NC in ART-suppressed PLWH were observed.
source: Moreover, no significant differences between the killing of TCD32dim and TCD32− by NC in ART-suppressed PLWH were observed (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: TCD32dim cells from ART-suppressed PLWH were significantly more resistant to ADCC in comparison to their negative cell counterparts.
source: However, and in concordance with results in Figure 1A and C, TCD32dim cells from ART-suppressed PLWH were significantly more resistant to ADCC in comparison to their negative cell counterparts (median % ADCC killing normalized to NC of 19.66 vs 35.85 for TCD32dim and TCD32−, respectively) (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H with statistical comparison.

claim: A higher increase of HIV-RNA+ cells was observed in the TCD32dim fraction compared to TCD32− cells in all LRA treatment conditions.
source: We observed a higher increase of HIV-RNA+ cells in the TCD32dim fraction compared to TCD32− cells in all conditions and, within TCD32dim cells, HIV-RNA+ cells were more frequent after Romidepsin treatment compared to untreated cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNA FISH-flow assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Upregulation of CD32 expression upon treatment with several LRAs was evidenced in total CD4+ T cells.
source: Upregulation of CD32 expression upon the treatment with several LRAs was evidenced in total CD4+ T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A higher frequency of viral reactivated cells (p24+ cells) was found within the TCD32dim fraction.
source: Also in line with our previous results, we found a higher frequency of viral reactivated cells (p24+ cells) within the TCD32dim fraction (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Viral-reactivated cells were susceptible to ADCC with a median of 30% increase in the ADCC activity compared with the NC activity.
source: After the NK killing assays, viral-reactivated cells, in general, were susceptible to ADCC (Figure 2D, ART+LRA+NK+plasma condition) with a median of 30% increase in the ADCC activity compared with the NC activity (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: There was an increase in the expression of CD32 after latency disruption, which constituted a significant fraction of the total pool of viral reactivated cells.
source: We observed an increase in the expression of CD32 after latency disruption, which constituted a significant fraction of the total pool of viral reactivated cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The population of viral-reactivated cells expressing CD32 was refractory to ADCC and even increased after the ADCC assays.
source: Remarkably, this population was refractory to ADCC and even increased after the ADCC assays (condition with plasma) (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: TCD32dim cells showed a higher pattern of ADCC resistance compared to the total HIV-reactivated cells.
source: Thus, concordantly with previous results, TCD32dim cells showed a higher pattern of ADCC resistance compared to the total HIV-reactivated cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: HIV induced higher expression of MICA/B, ULBP-1, and CD155 in infected cells compared to uninfected cells.
source: Overall, we observed that, despite HIV induced higher expression of MICA/B, ULBP-1, and CD155 in infected cells compared to uninfected cells, only a small proportion of infected cells expressed these activating ligands (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Only a small proportion of infected cells expressed the activating ligands MICA/B, ULBP-1, and CD155.
source: Overall, we observed that, despite HIV induced higher expression of MICA/B, ULBP-1, and CD155 in infected cells compared to uninfected cells, only a small proportion of infected cells expressed these activating ligands (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The ligand HLA-E was found to be expressed in a significantly higher proportion of infected cells (median of 12.0% in HIV-infected cells vs 9.4% in uninfected cells, p=0.002).
source: In contrast, the ligand HLA-E was found to be expressed in a significantly higher proportion of infected cells (median of 12.0% in HIV-infected cells vs 9.4% in uninfected cells, p=0.002) (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D with statistical analysis.

claim: HLA-E expression was 2-fold significantly higher in HIV-infected TCD32dim compared to infected TCD32− cells (median of 22.2% and 11.0%, respectively, p<0.0001).
source: However, HLA-E expression was 2-fold significantly higher in HIV-infected TCD32dim compared to infected TCD32− cells (median of 22.2% and 11.0%, respectively, p<0.0001), and differences in MFI were also detected (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and H with statistical analysis.

claim: In the absence of any viral infection, TCD32dim cells showed intrinsically higher HLA-E expression.
source: Of note, in the absence of any viral infection, TCD32dim cells showed intrinsically higher HLA-E expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells expressing the molecule HLA-E were particularly resistant to NK-mediated killing.
source: Of note, as previously reported (Pereira et al., 2019; Ward et al., 2004), cells expressing the molecule HLA-E were particularly resistant to NK-mediated killing (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3L and citations to prior research.

claim: Infected TCD32dim cells expressing any of the activating NK ligands were more refractory to both NK-mediated immune responses.
source: However, infected TCD32dim cells expressing any of the activating NK ligands were more refractory to both NK-mediated immune responses (Figure 3M–P).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3M–P.

claim: After incubation with plasma containing HIV-unspecific immunocomplexes, there was a decrease in the total number of HIV-specific molecules (A32 mAb) able to bind to TCD32dim cells.
source: After incubation with plasma containing HIV-unspecific immunocomplexes (ICs), we found a decrease in the total number of HIV-specific molecules (A32 mAb) able to bind to TCD32dim cells (Figure 4A–B), but such effect was not observed in the TCD32− population (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: The decrease in HIV-specific antibody binding to TCD32dim cells after plasma incubation was not observed in the TCD32− population.
source: After incubation with plasma containing HIV-unspecific immunocomplexes (ICs), we found a decrease in the total number of HIV-specific molecules (A32 mAb) able to bind to TCD32dim cells (Figure 4A–B), but such effect was not observed in the TCD32− population (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was a significantly higher frequency of TCD32dim – NK doublets compared to TCD32− cells.
source: We observed a significantly higher frequency of TCD32dim – NK doublets compared to TCD32− cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: FACS-sorted and gp120-coated TCD32dim cells triggered a less potent NK degranulation than their negative counterparts.
source: Indeed, when we tested the capacity of FACS-sorted and gp120-coated TCD32dim cells to activate NK cells, we observed that these cells triggered a less potent NK degranulation than their negative counterparts (Figure 4E), whileIFN-γ was equally induced in both cases (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: HIV-infected cells, and in particular infected cells expressing CD32dim, had higher proliferative potential measured by the expression of Ki67 (median of 6.67% vs 4.62% for TCD32dim and TCD32−, respectively).
source: First, we observed that HIV-infected cells, and in particular infected cells expressing CD32dim, had higher proliferative potential measured by the expression of Ki67 (median of 6.67% vs 4.62% for TCD32dim and TCD32−, respectively) (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The addition of plasma from an HIV-infected patient induced significant proliferation of infected TCD32dim cells (median of 7.52% vs 12.80% for basal condition and plasma HIV+, respectively).
source: Importantly, we observed that the addition of plasma from an HIV-infected patient (containing a high titer of Igs), induced significant proliferation of infected TCD32dim cells (median of 7.52% vs 12.80% for basal condition and plasma HIV+, respectively), which was not significant when Fc receptor blockers were added to the culture (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The proliferation induced by HIV+ plasma in TCD32dim cells was not significant when Fc receptor blockers were added to the culture.
source: Importantly, we observed that the addition of plasma from an HIV-infected patient (containing a high titer of Igs), induced significant proliferation of infected TCD32dim cells (median of 7.52% vs 12.80% for basal condition and plasma HIV+, respectively), which was not significant when Fc receptor blockers were added to the culture (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No effect on cell proliferation was observed after the addition of plasma from an HIV-negative donor.
source: Of note, no effect was observed after the addition of plasma from an HIV-negative donor (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cell proliferation was unchanged in the infected TCD32− population after plasma addition.
source: In contrast, cell proliferation was unchanged in the infected TCD32− population (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: IL-15 enhanced the performance of NK cells against the total gp120-coated CD4+ T cell population.
source: As expected and previously reported (Garrido et al., 2018), we observed an enhanced performance of NK cells against the total gp120-coated CD4+ T cell population when treated with IL-15, and to a lesser extent with IFN-α.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to Garrido et al., 2018.

claim: Neither IL-15 nor IFN-α was able to enhance the ADCC response against T CD32dim-infected cells.
source: However, neither IL-15 nor IFN-α was able to enhance the ADCC response against T CD32dim-infected cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CD32 expression on productively HIV-infected cells is associated with a reduced susceptibility to ADCC activity by NK cells.
source: Remarkably, we postulate a pivotal role of ADCC-NK in shaping the HIV reservoir during ART, being a novel route to avoid NK cell effector immunity by HIV-reservoir cells. We found that the expression of the molecule CD32 on productively HIV-infected cells is associated with a reduced susceptibility to ADCC activity by NK cells.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple experimental findings.

claim: When infected ex vivo, CD32-expressing cells express higher levels of the molecule HLA-E, which also limits NK-mediated killing.
source: Furthermore, when infected ex vivo, these cells express higher levels of the molecule HLA-E, which also limits NK-mediated killing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased HLA-E expression on infected CD32+ cells.

claim: Upon interaction with immune complexes, CD32-expressing infected cells' capacity to bind to HIV-specific antibodies decreases, while gaining the potential to proliferate.
source: Last, upon interaction with immune complexes, their capacity to bind to HIV-specific antibodies decreases, while gaining the potential to proliferate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced antibody binding and increased Ki67 expression after immune complex engagement.

claim: A significant proportion of HIV-latently infected cells expressed CD32 upon viral reactivation.
source: Considering that a significant proportion of HIV-latently infected cells expressed CD32 upon viral reactivation, as shown here and reported before (Grau-Expósito et al., 2019), these cells will indeed benefit from these described NK immune evasion mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from this study and citation to prior work.

claim: CD32 is expressed during latent and transcriptionally-active HIV infection.
source: However, the Fcγ receptor CD32 is perhaps one of the most promising HIV reservoir markers, since it is expressed during latent (Descours et al., 2017; Darcis et al., 2020) and transcriptionally-active infection (Abdel-Mohsen et al., 2018; Vásquez et al., 2019; Noto et al., 2018; Huot et al., 2021); it has been localized in main tissue reservoirs such as the cervical tissue (Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019), lymph nodes (Abdel-Mohsen et al., 2018; Noto et al., 2018) and the gastrointestinal tract (Vásquez et al., 2019) and, in some cases, it has been associated with a very prominent enrichment for HIV DNA (Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019; Descours et al., 2017; Darcis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: CD32 has been localized in main tissue reservoirs such as the cervical tissue, lymph nodes and the gastrointestinal tract.
source: However, the Fcγ receptor CD32 is perhaps one of the most promising HIV reservoir markers, since it is expressed during latent (Descours et al., 2017; Darcis et al., 2020) and transcriptionally-active infection (Abdel-Mohsen et al., 2018; Vásquez et al., 2019; Noto et al., 2018; Huot et al., 2021); it has been localized in main tissue reservoirs such as the cervical tissue (Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019), lymph nodes (Abdel-Mohsen et al., 2018; Noto et al., 2018) and the gastrointestinal tract (Vásquez et al., 2019) and, in some cases, it has been associated with a very prominent enrichment for HIV DNA (Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019; Descours et al., 2017; Darcis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In some cases, CD32 has been associated with a very prominent enrichment for HIV DNA.
source: However, the Fcγ receptor CD32 is perhaps one of the most promising HIV reservoir markers, since it is expressed during latent (Descours et al., 2017; Darcis et al., 2020) and transcriptionally-active infection (Abdel-Mohsen et al., 2018; Vásquez et al., 2019; Noto et al., 2018; Huot et al., 2021); it has been localized in main tissue reservoirs such as the cervical tissue (Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019), lymph nodes (Abdel-Mohsen et al., 2018; Noto et al., 2018) and the gastrointestinal tract (Vásquez et al., 2019) and, in some cases, it has been associated with a very prominent enrichment for HIV DNA (Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019; Descours et al., 2017; Darcis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cantero-Pérez et al., 2019; Descours et al., 2017; Darcis et al., 2020.

claim: CD32 expressed on CD4+ T cells is fully functional.
source: While CD32 expressed on CD4+ T cells is fully functional (Holgado et al., 2018; Engelhardt et al., 1995), many questions remain unknown regarding the expression dynamics and function, in particular during HIV pathogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Holgado et al., 2018; Engelhardt et al., 1995.

claim: CD32+CD4+ T cells were strongly increased in LNs, spleen, and intestine during SIV mac infection in non-human primates.
source: In a recent study with SIV-infected non-human primates, CD32+CD4+ T cells were strongly increased in LNs, spleen, and intestine during SIV mac infection, were enriched in markers often expressed on HIV-infected cells, and contained higher levels of actively transcribed SIV RNA (Huot et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huot et al., 2021.

claim: Cell proliferation is one of the most important mechanisms of cell reservoir maintenance in long-term ART-suppressed PLWH.
source: In this sense, cell proliferation is one of the most important mechanisms of cell reservoir maintenance in long-term ART-suppressed PLWH (Chomont et al., 2009; Gantner et al., 2020; Simonetti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chomont et al., 2009; Gantner et al., 2020; Simonetti et al., 2016.

claim: CD4+ T cell activation occurs upon CD32 ligation with antibodies or aggregated IgG.
source: Inherent proliferative capacity of this subset has recently been reported in a study demonstrating CD4+ T cell activation upon CD32 ligation with antibodies or aggregated IgG (Holgado et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Holgado et al., 2018.

claim: NK cell immune pressure leads to viral sequence evolution.
source: In this sense, it has been reported that NK cell immune pressure leads to viral sequence evolution (Alter et al., 2011), and HLA-mediated immune resistance mechanisms have been previously identified in productively HIV-infected cells (Cohen et al., 1999; Bonaparte and Barker, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alter et al., 2011.

claim: HLA-mediated immune resistance mechanisms have been previously identified in productively HIV-infected cells.
source: In this sense, it has been reported that NK cell immune pressure leads to viral sequence evolution (Alter et al., 2011), and HLA-mediated immune resistance mechanisms have been previously identified in productively HIV-infected cells (Cohen et al., 1999; Bonaparte and Barker, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cohen et al., 1999; Bonaparte and Barker, 2004.

claim: Resistance of reservoir cells to HIV-specific cytotoxic T cells has been reported.
source: Moreover, resistance of reservoir cells to HIV-specific cytotoxic T cells has also been reported (Ren et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2018), and Nef has been identified as a key protein for the persistence of genetically intact HIV proviruses in effector memory CD4+ T cells (Duette et al., 2022), suggesting that viral persistence might be facilitated not only by cell proliferation mechanisms in the absence of viral antigen expression, but also by avoiding immune-mediated killing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ren et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2018.

claim: Nef has been identified as a key protein for the persistence of genetically intact HIV proviruses in effector memory CD4+ T cells.
source: Moreover, resistance of reservoir cells to HIV-specific cytotoxic T cells has also been reported (Ren et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2018), and Nef has been identified as a key protein for the persistence of genetically intact HIV proviruses in effector memory CD4+ T cells (Duette et al., 2022), suggesting that viral persistence might be facilitated not only by cell proliferation mechanisms in the absence of viral antigen expression, but also by avoiding immune-mediated killing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duette et al., 2022.

claim: Vpu reduces the presence of viral antigens susceptible to recognition by antibodies on the surface of infected cells.
source: For instance, Vpu reduces the presence of viral antigens susceptible to recognition by antibodies on the surface of infected cells (Arias et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arias et al., 2014.

claim: Vpu is responsible for the decreased expression of tetherin, a cellular host restriction factor that retains HIV virions on the cell surface, and therefore diminishes ADCC responses.
source: This accessory protein is responsible for the decreased expression of tetherin, a cellular host restriction factor that retains HIV virions on the cell surface, and therefore diminishes ADCC responses (Arias et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arias et al., 2014.

claim: Vpu and Nef downregulate CD4 expression on infected cells, preventing its interaction with Env trimers, which subsequently impedes the binding of ADCC-antibodies.
source: Moreover, Vpu and Nef downregulate CD4 expression on infected cells, preventing its interaction with Env trimers, which subsequently impedes the binding of ADCC-antibodies (Veillette et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Veillette et al., 2014.

claim: An antibody-dependent enhancement of infection has been extensively reported for Dengue infection.
source: This is not the first non-desirable effect of Igs identified in the context of an infectious disease; an antibody-dependent enhancement of infection has been extensively reported for Dengue infection (Martina et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martina et al., 2009.

claim: HIV infection maintains or even increases the expression of the non-classical HLA-E molecule, which may contribute to the inhibition of the NK cytotoxic response.
source: Furthermore, as previously reported by others, HIV infection maintains or even increases the expression of the non-classical HLA-E molecule, which may contribute to the inhibition of the NK cytotoxic response (Ward et al., 2004; Martini et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ward et al., 2004; Martini et al., 2005.

claim: HLA-E has been shown to impair ADCC against HIV-expressing cells, while impeding its interaction with NK cells improved the elimination of target cells.
source: In addition, HLA-E has been shown to impair ADCC against HIV-expressing cells, while impeding its interaction with NK cells improved the elimination of target cells (Ward et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ward et al., 2004.

claim: HIV chronic infection has a deleterious effect on NK cell function, which is not completely restored despite ART.
source: These results are in agreement with previous reports showing that HIV chronic infection has a deleterious effect on NK cell function, which is not completely restored despite ART (Nabatanzi et al., 2019; Lichtfuss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nabatanzi et al., 2019; Lichtfuss et al., 2012.

claim: IL-15 and IFN-α upregulate NKG2A on NK cells.
source: A plausible explanation would be the upregulation of NKG2A on NK cells mediated by these cytokines (Merino et al., 2019; Mori et al., 1998), which would further limit the killing of cells already expressing high levels of HLA-E, such as TCD32dim cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Merino et al., 2019; Mori et al., 1998.

claim: There is a decline of HIV-specific antibody levels in ART-treated PLWH.
source: A potential limitation of our study is the decline of HIV-specific antibody levels in ART-treated PLWH (Madhavi et al., 2015; Jensen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Madhavi et al., 2015; Jensen et al., 2015.

claim: Functional ADCC activity mediated by NK cells remains detectable in long-term virally-suppressed individuals.
